main_point.en: Jesus is worthy of our best worship.

christ_connection.en: The Passover, along with the temple and perpetual sacrifices, revealed God’s desire to be with His people and the way they could be made right with Him. These signs pointed to the greater way that God would restore people to Himself through Christ. All who trust in Jesus are forgiven and made right with God forever.

content.en: .13 The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. 14 In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there. 15 And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. 16 And he told those who sold the pigeons, “Take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.” 17 His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”

18 So the Jews said to him, “What sign do you show us for doing these things?” 19 Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” 20 The Jews then said, “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?” 21 But he was speaking about the temple of his body. 22 When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken. 23 Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. 24 But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people 25 and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
Leaders: Your best offering in worship teaches students that God is worthy of their best worship.

“They’ve set up shop in the outer court of the temple, the court of the Gentiles. Their lust for money is interfering with the Gentiles’ coming to worship the one true God. They’ve trivialized the worship of God. When an unbeliever entered the temple and saw the commerce, he would assume the God of Israel is a prop used to extort people’s money. Jesus is angry because his Father’s house is being corrupted. Worship is being perverted. Kent Hughes wrote, ‘The way we worship reveals what we think about God.’ Jesus thought correctly about God. He perfectly understood the holiness, power, and authority of God. That is why he was so passionate about God’s house. . . . God’s people are in awe of him. God’s people worship him. Coming to God in faith requires turning from self-worship to true worship. If each Sunday is a narcissistic activity of self-worship, then you are walking in the footsteps of the temple merchants.”⁵

“As far as the money changers (2:14) are concerned, each Israelite who was part of the annual poll was expected to provide a half-shekel tax/offering to the temple (Ex. 30:13). Moreover, those who came from a distance instead of bringing offerings of animals or birds could bring money and purchase them from the temple staff, a practice that developed out of the alternative pattern provided in Deuteronomy 14:25. The payments of these items, however, could not be made in foreign currencies like Roman denarii, which contained pagan symbols and the images of emperors. Therefore the money had to be exchanged for appropriate temple currency. The result was that the temple also became a major money exchange or bank.”⁶

“The use of the term ‘sign’ here in this context of confrontation or demand by the Jews has a slightly different focus from the sign for believers as in 2:11. The Jewish challenge was for proof of either Jesus’s right to make a particular statement (6:30) or to do a particular act (2:18). The demand for such a sign was in effect the demand for Jesus to justify himself in their eyes. In such contexts in John, Jesus refused the requests. He readily argued with the Jews, but he refused to become a magician performing signs for their benefit.”⁷

The priesthood was incredibly corrupt before and during Jesus’s lifetime. Bribes determined the next high priest instead of lots drawn by members of the Levite tribe. Wealthy Sadducees paid to be appointed in exchange for keeping peace with Rome and enforcing Roman law; as compensation, they benefited from temple tithes and animal sales. Understanding this corruption helps us understand Jesus’s actions in the temple—His Father’s house. God required spotless sacrifices. But the priesthood, the Annas family, inspected all sacrifices and frequently denied them, forcing people to purchase available animals right there in the temple, specifically in the Court of the Gentiles, at insanely inflated prices. The Annases profited off of the Jews who made the pilgrimage to Jerusalem for Passover, the annual festival celebrating the exodus from Egypt. Not only did they inflate prices, but they also charged temple taxes. The market-like atmosphere hindered Gentiles from worshiping. This context set the stage for Jesus’s righteous indignation at what the sacrificial system of atonement had become—a system He came to replace with His own body, the Lamb of God.

God’s holiness refers to His uniqueness in being separate from all He has created. The Hebrew word for “holy” means “separate” or “set apart.” God’s holiness also refers to His absolute purity. God is unstained by the evil of the world. His goodness is perfect, and the moral code we find in the Scriptures is a reflection of His holy nature. As people made in God’s image, we are called to holiness.

God, we want to honor you in our worship. Only because of Jesus can we come before you, righteous and forgiven. Help us to remember your holiness and your worthiness every time we come before you in worship. We offer our hearts as a sacrifice, surrendering them fully to you.

question.en: In 2022, one of the deadliest outbreaks of bird flu killed tens of millions of egg-laying hens. How did this affect us? The cost of eggs skyrocketed 59.5%!⁸

instructions.en:
These optional activities are designed to help your students interact. You’ll find a Discussion Activity and a Cultural Connection, which touches on a relevant topic in today’s teen culture. Each group is different, so adapt these activities to fit your group’s needs. The goal is for

Ask the following questions, allowing time for students to share responses:

question.en: Have you ever wanted something so much that you would pay more than it was worth to get it? (ex: concert tickets, shoes, collectibles)
Why are we willing to pay way more for certain things?
What is something you paid too much for and then regretted it?

content.en: We make sacrifices for what matters to us. If something is valuable to us, then we’re willing to go to great lengths to have it or to protect it. God deserves our best worship, but so often, we withhold it or give it away to lesser “gods” and idols. Jesus’s sacrifice was enough to cover us; He paid the price for our sin so that we can enjoy relationship with God.

cultural_connection.en: What is worship? How do we worship God the right way? We use the word “worship” a lot in Christian culture, but the word even bleeds into secular, or worldly, culture. We say things like, “She worships the ground he walks on” and make people, brands, and activities our idols. Only God is worthy of worship, but we often bow before lesser “gods”—false gods that can’t save us, gods that lead us away from the one true God and to destruction. Worship is giving God the glory and praise He deserves; worship involves our words, but even more, worship is bowing our hearts before the Lord and living in submission to Him. Here’s how we know we’re worshiping God the right way: We examine what our love and adoration point to; we examine what we’re devoted to; we ask if our heart is divided between God and anything else. And if it is, we lay that thing down in surrender. Worship requires us to surrender our hearts, minds, and actions to the only One who is worthy.

question.en: When someone disrespects you or someone you love, how do you typically react?

answer.en: A core human desire is the need to feel valued. Most of us have been disrespected at some point, causing us to feel small and invisible. Maybe someone said something harmful about our character or insulted our family. Some of us handle being disrespected better than watching family members, people we love, or people who are vulnerable be mistreated. We rise up to defend them and may feel immediate anger, a desire for revenge, or the need to fix the situation. In the moment, we just want to restore value to ourselves and the people we care about.

question.en: What does Jesus’s reaction help you understand about anger?

answer.en: Many of us misunderstand anger, believing it’s a sin. While anger can lead to sin, it’s an emotion—one God feels perfectly and righteously. God is slow to anger (Ps. 103:8). Paul instructed believers to “be angry and do not sin” (Eph. 4:26). This means that we can be angry without sinning. How? Selfish anger and righteous anger have different motives. Righteous anger stirs us to action and motivates us to stand against sin and injustice. Jesus displayed righteous anger. His anger wasn’t rooted in revenge or pride, like ours so often is, but in respect for God’s holiness, with the goal of restoring acceptable worship in the temple.

question.en: In what ways do we cheapen worship or treat God’s house with disrespect?

answer.en: Leaders: Share context that set the stage for this event. The sacrificial system in the Old Testament and in Jesus’s time was broken. What God intended as provision for humans to experience forgiveness of sin transitioned into a money-making scheme that took advantage of people. What was supposed to be worshipful morphed into a corrupted show, distracting people from worship. God demanded a better sacrifice than what the people were bringing—even with inflated prices. If we aren’t careful, we can be guilty of cheapening worship too. How? By appearing to worship God but being far from Him in our hearts. By looking the part at church but living like the world. By singing worship songs under bright lights and fog but not living the way God calls us to live in His Word. By making worship and church about us instead of God. By not offering Him our best. Here’s the truth: Only pure sacrifice makes us right with God and enables us to worship Him. God’s holiness demands a better sacrifice than we could ever bring. Our better sacrifice is Jesus. He is the only acceptable sacrifice. He covered our sin fully, permanently. When we make worship about us rather than God, we cheapen His sacrifice.

question.en: Why did the Jews ask for a sign (v. 18)? Is there ever an okay reason to ask God for a sign?

answer.en: After Jesus cleared the temple courts, the Jews asked for a sign. In other words, they asked for proof of Jesus’s authority to make a claim that the temple was His Father’s house. Why? When Jesus said this, He claimed to be God’s Son, and this was a big statement that could warrant investigation from Jewish leaders. They didn’t want a sign so that they could believe. They asked for a sign out of a desire to prove Jesus was a fraud. Other times in the Bible, God did sometimes honor the request for a sign (Ex. Gideon, Abraham’s servant). The difference was that God provided these signs to strengthen people’s faith and to empower them to accomplish His plan. We can ask God to confirm His will for us while consulting His Word first, seeking Him in prayer, and seeking wise advice from godly mentors.

question.en: What did Jesus realize about many of the people who believed in Him after the signs? What does this type of belief look like today?

answer.en: Because Jesus is omniscient, or all-knowing, He saw through the people’s exterior and knew their hearts. Their “belief” was dependent on signs Jesus performed and not in the truth that He was the Messiah, the Son of God. Like them, we often chase God’s works over knowing Him. We believe only if God does what we ask of Him. Our belief isn’t rooted in faith—in absolute assurance that Jesus is Lord. If attached to signs, our belief unravels when life hurts, when healing doesn’t come, when we feel like God doesn’t answer our prayers. But belief rooted in faith, in the assurance of who Jesus is and in the hope of the gospel, is unwavering. Signs are unnecessary because Jesus’s life, death, and resurrection are enough.

question.en: Why does Jesus compare Himself to the temple?

answer.en: The temple was crucial to the Jews’ identity. The temple provided a center for sacrifice and a way for God to dwell among His people. The temple had been destroyed and rebuilt, so Jesus’s statement sounded like a radical threat. But Jesus spoke of Himself as the temple. Jesus is God, and He dwelled among His people as the center for sacrifice—as the sacrifice. He surrendered His body, allowing it to fall, but after three days, He raised back to life! The temple was always a shadow of Jesus, the better temple.

question.en: When have you felt like you didn’t have anything good to bring to God? How can you rest in Jesus’s perfect sacrifice?

answer.en: God is holy. He can’t accept half-hearted, insincere worship. Our cheap sacrifices can never be worthy enough for us to enter God’s holy presence; our best sacrifices rooted in our own goodness can never be enough either. God requires complete surrender, which can feel a little intimidating, right? Here’s the other part: God requires our best but gave His Son to be our best offering. He demands everything, but Jesus lowered Himself to satisfy the demand and was everything on our behalf (Phil. 2:7-8). Jesus’s perfect sacrifice covers us and atones for our sin. He purchased our freedom and our rest. So, we don’t have to strive to be worthy because the blood of Jesus makes us worthy! God still deserves our best, but instead of striving to earn salvation, our best is rooted in gratitude for what Jesus has already done. His work on the cross was enough. And now, we have the privilege of living our lives as offerings of praise.

content.en:
If you could have one superpower, what would it be? A lot of really cool options are available to choose from, like being invisible, being able to fly, traveling through time, or having super strength. What about mind reading, though? It may sound cool at first, but when you start thinking about it, would we really want to know what people are thinking?

The only person who can read our minds and see our hearts is Jesus. He knows each person inside and out. What’s incredible is that He still loves us, even when our thoughts are sinful, selfish, and ugly. Jesus doesn’t look for perfection in us; He looks for faithfulness. In today’s Scripture, we see a picture of people who were obsessed with looking perfect, but who didn’t truly love God and love people. They loved self-image more than their neighbor. So, Jesus called them out. He was able to do this because He is God. He saw through the people’s exterior and straight to their hearts. He sees through our attempts to look the part too.

Jesus wants His children to bring their imperfections to Him. When we do that, we show a desire for God to transform our hearts and our minds. Many of us may not come to God with honesty because we feel ashamed on the inside. But God can handle it! We can put our trust in Him, and He will take care of the rest. You may be tempted to stay away from God because of shame you feel over something you’ve done. God wants to heal your heart; He wants to transform you and give you peace. God sees you and loves you. No matter how ugly your heart and mind are, you can go to God in honesty and ask Him to make you new.

question.en: In what ways have you tried to appear one way on the outside but your inside was the opposite?
What sin and shame do you need to bring to God so you can truly live for him?

prayer.en: Lord, you desire for a transformed heart to drive my outside actions. Show me what this looks like in this season of my life and give me the strength to move in that direction.

content.en:
The kitchen table is meant to be the place in the house for eating meals. On occasion though, we might eat on the couch or in our bed. We’ve probably all spilled our food or drink and ruined a good piece of furniture too. Cleaning up the mess usually takes more than some hot water and a washcloth and requires the best cleaning supplies we can find because nothing else will do the trick.

Our hearts are a lot like that mess we made from the food we spilled. Because of our sin, our hearts are stained beyond what we can fix. In fact, nothing can fix it—not our good works, moral living, or serving others. Jesus is the only One who can clean and remove the stain of sin for good. Today’s verses in Isaiah speak about the cleansing work Jesus does. As we discussed yesterday, Jesus sees the inside of our hearts and diagnoses our problem. He doesn’t leave us in that diagnosis without hope for healing. When we bring our sin problem to Him with honesty and desperation, He wipes it away. We receive a clean slate and are able to live the way God intended us to live.

That’s the power of the gospel message! The sacrifice Jesus made on the cross is more than enough to clean our sinful stains. When He died and shed His blood for us, He took on all the sins of the world. Then, He appeared to hundreds of people and went to heaven. He sent His Holy Spirit to live in us so we can be clean and live with new purpose! Thank you, Jesus, for making us clean!

question.en: Think about sins you currently struggle with. How have you tried to clean up those sins on your own?
What is one step you can take today to allow Jesus to cover your stains with his grace?

prayer.en: Lord, thank you for sending your son to the cross. You chose to send Jesus because you love us. Teach me to remember this truth every day.

content.en:
There is nothing like having a Saturday to sleep in, watch TV, and enjoy some good breakfast. After a long week of school and extra activities, we need those Saturdays at times. Actually, we need them more than we think! God created us to work, but He also created us for rest. They both matter, and one doesn’t work well without the other. We have all felt the tension of work and rest; we’ve all experienced fatigue that comes from living without balance.

This idea of work and rest also connects to our spiritual lives. God’s people in the Old Testament felt this tension too. Before Jesus came to earth, God’s people had to keep the law and make sacrifices for their sins. Can you imagine how tired God’s people must have been at times? Maybe even how they worried if they were doing it “right” or doing “enough”? God still provided them rest by giving them a weekly sabbath. The word Sabbath means to cease and stop. God still commands us to cease and stop all our work to just rest. But rest doesn’t come easy for a lot of us. We struggle to stop; some of us avoid pausing because doing so allows us time to think, and maybe there are things we don’t want to think about. Maybe we find too much satisfaction in our work. But God intended for us to rest. Our physical rest points to the spiritual rest God offers us through His Son, Jesus. The book of Hebrews was written for Christians who were used to earning righteousness through following the law. The people needed to receive the spiritual rest Jesus brought through the cross and resurrection. They could stop trying so hard and striving for righteousness because Jesus fulfilled the requirements of the law and earned their rest. He offers us rest too. The weekly Sabbath is a reminder that we don’t have to work for our salvation. We can rest in what Jesus did.

question.en: What connections do you see between physical rest and spiritual rest?
Do you have at least one day a week to slow down and remember Jesus and the gifts he has given you? If not, what needs to change?

prayer.en: Lord, thank you for the rest that comes through a relationship with Jesus Christ. Help me to receive and live in that rest and set aside the time to remember what you’ve done for me.

content.en:
Sometimes churches use the word worship only when referring to a service on a Sunday morning or at youth group, a retreat, or at camp—when music plays, people sing, and someone teaches from the Bible. Although that’s not wrong, worship is much more than a service and singing songs. Because many of us are used to hearing worship described this way, we limit worship. Worship is actually a lifestyle! We worship who or what our thoughts and attention focus on the most. The question isn’t if we will worship but who or what will we worship?

Today’s passage tells us to offer a continual sacrifice of praise to God. At times, praise comes easily for us; at other times, praising God can feel like a sacrifice because life hurts. In those seasons, we honor God by giving Him glory despite walking through suffering or disappointment. Our sacrificial worship pleases God because we were made to give Him glory— when life is good and when life is painful. Why? Because God’s goodness never changes and isn’t dependent on our circumstances. So, how can we do this? First, we can worship God with our words, consistently expressing gratitude for who He is and what He has done for us. When you talk to others, you can tell them how Jesus gave you new life and purpose. Next, we can praise Him by being kind and generous with people in need. Worshiping with our words and our actions is like a spiritual offering, showing that Jesus has changed our hearts. When we praise God, we take the attention off of ourselves and direct it to Him. We celebrate His goodness and His glory.

question.en: If you were to take an honest look at your life right now, who or what do you worship the most?
How can you begin to see your worship of Jesus as a lifestyle instead of an event?

prayer.en: Lord, show me how my worship falls short of giving you the glory and praise you deserve. Lead me toward a daily lifestyle of worship so I can live each day with joy and purpose.

content.en:
What’s the difference between doing what’s right and having a right heart? We can do something good for others and appear to care deeply for them while really hating them in our hearts. We can fool others when we do good works for all the wrong reasons: to get attention, to please others, to earn forgiveness.

The people of Judah looked like they were doing all the right things, but God saw past their actions to the real problem in their hearts. The prophet Isaiah wrote to the people of Judah, who had lived a double life for years and years. We see in chapter 1 just how bad the situation was. Although God had not abandoned His people, they had abandoned Him over and over. Because of this, God allowed the destruction of their temple and their city. God desired for His people to be made new. In chapter 6, Isaiah encountered God and saw his own sin in all its heaviness and ugliness. He saw God for who He was too—holy. This encounter with the holy God changed him forever. God then told Isaiah to go and preach to Judah. Judah had a heart problem. Because their hearts weren’t clean, their worship wasn’t meaningful to God and fell short of what God demanded—of what He deserved. Isaiah confronted this problem but also assured the people that a Messiah would come to cleanse their hearts for good.

Does your heart resemble Judah’s? Does your worship fall short of what God demands and deserves, which is everything? Confess this to God. Receive His grace. If you do, God will send you out with great purpose. You’ll never be the same!

question.en: How did isaiah respond to encountering God? Do you respond to God in this way? Why or why not?
When have you done good works—even godly actions— for the wrong reasons? What needs to change in your heart?

prayer.en: Lord, help me to see my sin for what it is and to see you for who you are. Thank you for loving me, forgiving me, and sending me out for a great purpose!
